Forces Inside Materials

When a load is applied to a component, forces are transmitted through its internal structure. To predict whether a component will survive in service, engineers calculate stress, strain, and Young's modulus. These three quantities are linked by Hooke's Law behaviour — understanding them lets engineers choose the right material and the correct cross-section for each job.

Key Fact

Stress: σ = F ÷ A (N/m²). Strain: ε = ΔL ÷ L (no unit). Young's modulus: E = σ ÷ ε (N/m²). The rearrangement step — making F, A, ΔL or L the subject — is the skill that separates full marks from zero on multi-step calculation questions.

Stress (σ)

Stress describes how concentrated a force is within a material. The formula is σ = F ÷ A, where σ (sigma) is stress in N/m², F is the applied tensile or compressive force in Newtons, and A is the original cross-sectional area in m². A thinner rod has a smaller area, so the same force produces higher stress — this is why thin cables snap before thick ones under equal loads.

Rearranging the stress formula is essential. If the question asks for the force needed to produce a given stress: F = σ × A. If the question asks for the area needed to keep stress below a limit: A = F ÷ σ. Always identify which variable the question is asking you to find before substituting any numbers.

Strain (ε)

Strain describes how much a material stretches (or compresses) relative to its original length. The formula is ε = ΔL ÷ L, where ΔL (delta L) is the change in length and L is the original length. Both must be in the same unit — the result is dimensionless (no unit). A strain of 0.002 means the material has stretched by 0.2% of its original length.

A steel suspension rod is 2.0 m long and has a circular cross-section of diameter 12 mm. It carries a tensile load of 45 000 N. When the load is applied, the rod extends by 1.2 mm.

Part 1 — Stress:

Step 1: Find the radius — r = 12 ÷ 2 = 6 mm = 0.006 m

Step 2: Find the area — A = π × (0.006)² = π × 0.000036 = 1.131 × 10⁻⁴ m²

Step 3: Stress — σ = F ÷ A = 45 000 ÷ 1.131 × 10⁻⁴ = 3.98 × 10⁸ N/m² ≈ 398 MPa

Part 2 — Strain:

ΔL = 1.2 mm = 0.0012 m; L = 2.0 m

ε = ΔL ÷ L = 0.0012 ÷ 2.0 = 0.0006 (no unit — it is a pure ratio)

Young's Modulus (E)

Young's modulus is the ratio of stress to strain within the elastic (Hooke's Law) region. E = σ ÷ ε. It measures stiffness: a higher E means the material resists deformation more effectively. Steel has E ≈ 200 GPa; aluminium has E ≈ 70 GPa; rubber has E ≈ 0.01 GPa. Engineers select materials partly based on whether their stiffness suits the application.

Using the values from the suspension rod worked example: σ = 3.98 × 10⁸ N/m²; ε = 0.0006.

E = σ ÷ ε = 3.98 × 10⁸ ÷ 0.0006 = 6.63 × 10¹¹ N/m²

This value is higher than typical steel (200 GPa) — in an exam, a discrepancy like this would prompt you to check your area calculation. This illustrates why showing all working allows the examiner to award method marks even if the final value is not perfectly accurate.

Always quote Young's modulus in GPa (÷ by 10⁹) if the question asks for it: e.g. 6.63 × 10¹¹ ÷ 10⁹ = 663 GPa. State the unit explicitly.

Stress-Strain Graphs

The stress-strain graph shows how a material behaves from the first application of load until it fractures. The shape of the curve tells engineers whether a material is ductile or brittle.

Ductile materials (e.g. mild steel, copper): the graph shows a linear elastic region up to the yield point, then a plastic region where permanent deformation occurs, then gradual necking and fracture. The material gives clear warning before failure — useful in structural applications.

Brittle materials (e.g. cast iron, glass, ceramics): the graph is a short straight line up to a sudden fracture with no plastic region. No warning is given — the material snaps without distortion. Brittle materials are used where compressive loads dominate (e.g. bricks in walls) but avoided where tensile impact loads are possible.

Key Fact

The slope of the stress-strain graph in the elastic region equals Young's modulus (E = stress ÷ strain = rise ÷ run). A steeper slope means a stiffer material. The yield point is where the material moves from elastic (reversible) to plastic (permanent) deformation.

Factor of Safety

No material is perfect — manufacturing defects, unexpected overloads and environmental degradation all reduce a component's actual strength below its theoretical maximum. Engineers account for this uncertainty using the factor of safety (FoS). The formula is: FoS = yield stress ÷ working stress. A factor of safety of 3 means the component could theoretically withstand three times the intended load before yielding — providing a safety margin.

Factor-of-safety values depend on the application, the risks and the relevant standard. Higher values can mean heavier, more expensive components, so engineers choose a suitable safe value for the application.

Four Types of Motion

Mechanical systems transmit and transform movement. Before designing a mechanism you must identify what type of motion is needed at the output. There are four types that engineers work with every day.

Rotary motion is spinning around a fixed axis — a motor shaft, a gear, a wheel. Linear motion is movement in a straight line, such as the travel of a drill bit moving into a workpiece. Reciprocating motion is back-and-forth movement along a straight line — a piston, a saw blade or a needle in an industrial sewing machine. Oscillating motion is a swinging or rocking motion around a fixed point, like a pendulum or a windscreen wiper arm.

In the examination you must use the correct technical terms — answers like “goes round and round” or “goes sideways” are not credited. A motor produces rotary motion; a piston produces reciprocating motion.

Key Fact

The four types of motion are rotary (spinning around an axis), linear (straight line), reciprocating (back-and-forth straight line) and oscillating (swinging around a fixed point). Most mechanisms convert one type of motion into another.

Linkages and Conversion of Motion

A linkage is a set of rigid bars joined by pivots that transmits or changes the direction of movement. Engineers use linkages when they need to transmit force around corners, reverse direction, or change the shape of a motion path.

The simplest linkage is a reverse linkage (bell crank). Pushing one arm down causes the other arm to push outward — the motion direction changes by 90°. Bicycle brake levers use this principle: squeezing the handle pulls a cable that pushes brake pads against the wheel rim. A parallel linkage keeps two bars moving in the same direction — used in toy train pantographs and car suspension systems.

The crank and slider mechanism is the fundamental converter of rotary motion into reciprocating motion. A rotating crank pin is connected to a slider (piston) by a connecting rod. As the crank rotates, the slider moves back and forth. Every internal combustion engine uses this principle — the rotating crankshaft drives the pistons up and down.

The reverse is also possible: a reciprocating steam engine drives a piston back and forth, which turns a crankshaft via a connecting rod to produce rotary motion at the wheels. Engineers describe this as converting reciprocating to rotary motion.

Cams and Followers

A cam is a specially shaped piece that rotates and pushes a component called a follower up and down as it turns. The key principle: the position of the follower at any instant depends entirely on the radius of the cam at the point of contact. Where the cam radius is large, the follower is pushed up. Where the radius is small, the follower drops down. This is the examiner’s most-tested cam concept — you must be able to explain it, not just name it.

Key Fact

The follower’s position at any moment is determined by the cam profile — specifically the radius of the cam at the point of contact. A large radius pushes the follower high; a small radius lets it drop. The cam profile is therefore what engineers adjust to control the follower’s movement pattern.

Four cam profiles appear in engineering exam questions:

  • Pear cam — egg-shaped profile. The follower rises slowly to a maximum height and then drops quickly. Used in car engine valve timing, where a valve must open slowly and snap shut.
  • Eccentric (circular) cam — a circular disc with the pivot offset from the centre. As it rotates the follower rises and falls smoothly in a simple harmonic pattern. Used in pumps and simple oscillating machines.
  • Snail (drop) cam — the follower rises very gradually around most of the rotation, then drops almost vertically as it reaches the “snail’s tail” drop. Used in clock escapements and stamping machines where a sudden downward force is needed.
  • Heart cam — heart-shaped profile that converts the continuous rotation into a back-and-forth motion of equal rate in both directions. Used in mechanisms where a constant-rate reciprocation is needed.

Choosing the Right Mechanism

When an engineer needs to convert motion, they select the mechanism based on the motion required and the forces involved. To convert rotary to reciprocating: use a cam or a crank and slider. To change the direction of a force: use a linkage (bell crank, reverse linkage). To transmit rotary motion between shafts that are far apart or at an angle: use gears, chains or belts (covered in Lesson 3).

In an aero-engine control unit, precision cams govern the opening and closing of fuel valves, and their profiles are machined to very tight tolerances because a small timing error changes engine performance. The cam profile is machined to tolerances of ±0.005 mm because any deviation changes the valve timing and affects thrust output. This real-world context shows why understanding cam profiles matters beyond the classroom.

Why Surface Finish Matters

A surface finish does two things simultaneously: it protects the base material from corrosion and it gives the product its appearance. Both matter commercially: a rusted chassis is structurally weakened, and an ugly surface finish damages a brand. Surface finishing is the last manufacturing stage before a product leaves the factory, so faults here affect every unit that ships. Understanding which finish suits which material, environment and cost envelope is a key engineering decision that examiners test every year.

Surface Preparation

Every surface finishing process begins with preparation. Paint, dip coatings and electroplating all bond poorly to a surface contaminated with grease, rust, mill scale or dust. Standard preparation steps are: degrease (solvent or alkali wash), abrade (grit-blast or sandpaper to provide a mechanical key), rinse and dry. Skipping preparation is the most common cause of coating failure in industry. A well-prepared surface can make a cheap paint finish outperform an expensive electroplated coating applied to a dirty surface.

Painting and Spray Painting

Painting applies a liquid coating to the surface that dries or cures to form a continuous protective film. Spray painting uses compressed air to atomise paint into a fine mist that settles evenly across the surface. It is used on vehicle bodywork, metal furniture, machinery guarding and architectural steelwork. Multiple thin coats are better than one thick coat, which sags and cures unevenly. High-volume industrial lines use electrostatic spray guns that charge the paint droplets so they are attracted to the earthed metal workpiece, reducing overspray waste.

Advantages of painting: wide colour choice; low cost for low-volume work; can be applied on-site to large structures (e.g. the Forth Road Bridge). Limitations: can chip or scratch to expose bare metal, allowing corrosion to undercut the surrounding paint (the most common failure mode); requires ventilation and personal protective equipment (PPE) due to solvent fumes.

Key Fact

Paint can chip or scratch to expose bare metal. Once bare metal is exposed, corrosion undercuts the surrounding coating from underneath, spreading the failure zone. Galvanising (zinc coating) sacrificially protects even when scratched because zinc is more electrochemically active than iron and corrodes preferentially.

Dip Coating

Dip coating (sometimes called plastisol dipping or powder dip coating) involves heating the cleaned metal component to around 200 °C and then dipping it into a fluidised bed of thermoplastic powder (typically PVC or polyethylene). The hot metal melts the powder particles that contact it, building up a thick, rubbery coating. The component is then cured in an oven. Dishwasher racks, tool handles, garden-chair frames and cycle-basket wire forms are typical applications: the thick thermoplastic coating gives grip, insulates electrically, resists knocks and provides complete waterproofing.

Advantages over spray paint: the coating is much thicker (typically 1–3 mm vs 50–150 μm for paint), more chemically resistant, and resistant to impact without chipping. Limitations: colour range is narrower than paint; the process requires heating the component, so large structures cannot be dip-coated easily; it is more expensive than painting per unit for large flat surfaces where thin coverage is acceptable.

Extension: powder coating, polishing and anodising are not named in the specification, which lists painting, dip coating, electroplating and galvanising. They are included as background because you will meet them in workshops and industry.

Spray paint: solvent-based or water-based liquid; thin coat (50–150 μm); wide colour range; can chip; low cost; suitable for on-site and large structures.

Powder coating: thermosetting polymer powder applied by electrostatic gun and oven-cured; thin but very hard and scratch-resistant coat; good colour range; cannot be applied on-site; better than paint for chip resistance.

Dip coating: thermoplastic powder, component heated and dipped; very thick, tough, rubbery coat; limited colour range; good grip and electrical insulation; best for wire forms and handles.

For an extended-response evaluation question, linking the choice to specific properties (coating thickness, chip resistance, grip, cost) and a specific application always earns the most marks.

Electroplating

Electroplating uses electricity to deposit a thin, uniform layer of a metal onto the workpiece surface. The component to be plated is made the cathode (negative electrode) in an electrolytic cell; the plating metal (e.g. chromium, nickel, gold, copper, zinc) forms the anode (positive electrode). Current flows through the electrolyte solution, dissolving metal from the anode and depositing it on the cathode surface. Chromium plating on car bumpers and taps gives a mirror finish and excellent corrosion resistance. Gold plating on electrical contacts reduces contact resistance and prevents oxidation. Zinc electroplating (electrogalvanising) protects steel fasteners.

Advantages: very thin (1–50 μm), dimensionally precise coating that adds almost no thickness to machined surfaces; excellent surface finish and appearance; can deposit expensive metals (gold, platinum) very economically because the layer is so thin. Limitations: the plating bath and anodes must be managed carefully; wastewater from plating is chemically hazardous and requires specialist disposal; not suitable for complex internal cavities where current density is uneven.

Galvanising

Galvanising coats steel with a layer of zinc. The dominant method is hot-dip galvanising: clean, fluxed steel is submerged in a bath of molten zinc at approximately 450 °C. The zinc reacts with the steel to form a series of intermetallic alloy layers, bonded much more strongly than a paint film. Street furniture, motorway crash barriers, agricultural machinery and structural steelwork are galvanised as standard.

Galvanising has one property that paint lacks: sacrificial (cathodic) protection. Zinc is more electrochemically active than iron; if the zinc coating is scratched through to bare steel, the zinc around the scratch corrodes preferentially, protecting the exposed iron. The zinc “sacrifices itself” to protect the steel. Paint has no such mechanism — a scratch allows moisture to reach the steel and corrosion spreads under the coating.

Key Fact

Zinc is more electrochemically active than iron. When both are in contact with moisture, zinc corrodes preferentially (sacrificial protection), so even a scratch through the galvanised coating does not allow the underlying steel to rust. Paint has no electrochemical activity — a chip exposes bare steel directly to moisture.

Polishing and Anodising

Polishing removes surface roughness mechanically — using abrasive compounds, buffing wheels or electropolishing — to produce a reflective, smooth surface. It is used on cutlery, surgical instruments, jewellery and any part where appearance or hygiene demands a smooth surface (rough surfaces trap bacteria). Polishing alone does not protect against corrosion but prepares the surface for electroplating or lacquering.

Anodising is most commonly used on aluminium. Aluminium naturally forms a thin oxide layer that protects it from further corrosion, but anodising deliberately thickens this oxide layer using electrolysis. The anodised surface is hard, scratch-resistant and porous: dye can be absorbed into the pores before sealing, giving a wide range of colours. Laptop casings, window frames, bicycle components and camera bodies are commonly anodised. Unlike paint or plating, the anodised layer is part of the aluminium itself and cannot peel.

Ask three questions to choose the right finish: 1. What material is the workpiece? (Aluminium → anodising is most appropriate. Steel → galvanising, electroplating, paint or dip coating all possible.) 2. What environment will it face? (Outdoor, wet, salt spray → galvanising; food contact → electropolished stainless; decorative indoor → electroplating or paint.) 3. What is the production volume? (High volume → galvanising or electroplating bath; low volume or on-site → spray paint; small components needing grip → dip coating.)

For a 6- or 8-mark extended response comparing two surface finishes, the examiner rewards “similarities and key differences” rather than isolated bullet points about each finish. Always name the application, the mechanism of corrosion protection, the process steps and one limitation before concluding which is better for the specific scenario.

Why Engineering Drawing Matters

An engineering drawing is a precise, standardised communication — the universal language between a designer in Sheffield and a CNC machinist in Birmingham. It conveys every dimension, material, tolerance and surface finish needed to manufacture a component correctly, first time, without ambiguity. Without standardised conventions, the same drawing could be interpreted differently by different manufacturers, leading to parts that do not fit or assemblies that fail.

Key Fact

Third-angle orthographic projection (BS 8888) is the standard used in the UK and USA. Views are arranged so the plan sits above the front elevation, and the right end view sits to the right. The symbol is a truncated cone viewed from the right, showing two circles.

Orthographic Projection — Third Angle

Orthographic projection divides a 3D object into flat views. Third-angle projection (used in the UK per BS 8888) places each view on the same side as the viewer: the right-end view goes to the right of the front elevation, the plan (top view) goes above the front elevation.

Key line conventions on orthographic drawings:

  • Continuous thick lines — visible outlines and edges.
  • Hidden detail lines (dashed) — edges or features that are behind the viewed surface and cannot be seen directly. These allow internal features (holes, slots) to be shown without a section cut.
  • Centre lines (chain-dotted) — show the axis of symmetry for circular features, holes and cylindrical parts. Engineers use them to locate the centre for drilling or turning operations.

The title block appears in the lower right corner and records: part name, drawing number, material, scale, projection angle symbol, drawn-by name, date, and revision status. Tolerances may be stated globally in the title block (e.g. 'general tolerance ±0.5 mm unless otherwise stated') or as specific dimension annotations.

Isometric drawing shows a 3D object with vertical lines drawn vertically and two horizontal axes at 30° to the horizontal. All lines are drawn to their true length along these axes — there is no perspective foreshortening. Isometric drawings are used to give clients and assembly teams a realistic-looking view of a component without the distortion of true perspective.

Oblique drawing shows the front face as a true orthographic view, with depth lines drawn at 45° to the horizontal. It is simpler to construct than isometric drawing but looks less realistic because depth is not foreshortened.

Exploded views show the individual parts of an assembly separated along their assembly axes — each component is spaced out so the relationship between parts is clear. Exploded views are used in assembly instructions (e.g. flat-pack furniture, engine manuals) and parts catalogues.

Section views reveal internal features by showing the object as if it has been cut along a defined plane. The cut surface is shown with cross-hatching (diagonal lines at 45°). Section views eliminate the need for multiple hidden detail lines when internal geometry is complex — for example, the interior of a valve body or a housing with multiple bores.

CAD — Computer-Aided Design

Computer-aided design (CAD) has replaced manual drafting in professional engineering practice. There are two distinct modes:

2D CAD software produces flat drawings equivalent to manual orthographic drafting, but with the ability to copy, mirror, dimension automatically, and output directly to plotters or laser cutters. It is used for workshop drawings, PCB layout and sheet metal patterns.

3D CAD (solid modelling) builds a virtual three-dimensional model of the component. The designer specifies base sketches and applies features (extrude, revolve, cut, fillet). From the 3D model, all 2D orthographic drawings can be generated automatically. 3D models can also be used for: finite element analysis (virtual stress testing), rendering for client presentations, and direct export to CAM software for manufacture. Autodesk Fusion 360, SolidWorks, and Creo are widely used in schools and industry.

Key Fact

Advantages of CAD over manual drawing: faster modification (change a dimension and the whole drawing updates automatically), no redrawing needed; instant 2D view generation from a 3D model; export directly to CAM for manufacture with no manual data re-entry; reduced human error in dimensioning; renders and animations for client approval before manufacture begins.

CAM — Computer-Aided Manufacture

Computer-aided manufacture (CAM) uses CAD geometry and chosen manufacturing settings to create toolpaths. A post-processor turns them into machine instructions, often G-code, for the chosen equipment. The main CAM processes are:

  • CNC machining (Computer Numerical Control) — a CNC milling machine or lathe moves cutting tools along programmed paths to remove material from a solid block. CNC achieves high precision, repeatable tolerances, and can run 24/7 with minimal operator intervention. Used for: engine components, aerospace brackets, mould tools.
  • Laser cutting — a high-power laser beam follows a CAD-defined path to cut sheet materials (metals, acrylic, wood). Very precise, no tool wear, minimal cutting force. Used for: PCB stencils, sheet metal chassis parts, signage.
  • Vinyl cutting — a blade plotter cuts sheet vinyl or thin materials from a 2D CAD vector file. Used for: labels, decals, stencils.
  • 3D printing (additive manufacturing) — builds a component layer by layer from a 3D CAD model using materials such as PLA, ABS or metal powder. Particularly suited to rapid prototyping (testing a design concept quickly and cheaply before committing to expensive tooling) and complex internal geometries that cannot be machined. The Tesla Gigafactory uses additive manufacturing for prototype components.
  • PCB routing — a small CNC mill removes copper tracks from a coated PCB blank to produce a custom printed circuit board from a CAD layout file.

Impact of Modern Engineering Technology on Society and the Environment

Examiners award marks specifically for developed points that link mechanism to impact — not just for naming an impact. Structure your answer around three dimensions: production, society and environment.

Production impacts: CAD/CAM reduces lead times from design to manufactured part; CNC automation reduces the need for skilled manual operators on repetitive tasks; digital designs can be shared globally and manufactured locally, compressing supply chains; rapid prototyping reduces the cost and time of early-stage design iteration.

Social impacts: automation can displace routine machining jobs but creates demand for higher-skilled roles (CNC programmers, design engineers, robotics technicians); engineering exports contribute to the national economy and provide jobs in companies such as BAE Systems and Rolls-Royce; improved product quality and reliability (e.g. in medical devices, vehicles) enhances quality of life; improved safety in hazardous processes through robot automation.

Environmental impacts: CNC precision reduces material waste compared to manual machining; 3D printing produces only the material needed (near-net-shape manufacture), reducing off-cuts; however, energy consumption in manufacturing facilities is significant; increased production capacity can accelerate resource depletion. Engineers apply the 6Rs framework (Rethink, Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repair, Recycle) to minimise these impacts across the product life cycle.

Rethink: redesign the product from the start to use less material or a more sustainable process. Refuse: decline to use materials or processes with unacceptable environmental impact. Reduce: use less material per component — near-net-shape processes like 3D printing minimise off-cuts. Reuse: design components for disassembly so they can be used again (e.g. remanufacturing used engine parts). Repair: design for maintainability so products can be serviced rather than discarded. Recycle: ensure end-of-life materials are recovered — steel, aluminium and copper are all commercially recycled at high rates.

What Is Additive Manufacturing?

Additive manufacturing is the opposite of cutting or drilling: instead of removing material, you build a part up, one thin layer at a time. A digital 3D model (usually saved as an STL file) is sliced into hundreds of horizontal layers by software, and the machine deposits or fuses material along each slice until the full shape is complete. Because no specialist tooling — moulds, dies, jigs — is required, a new design can go from computer screen to physical object in hours rather than weeks.

Key Fact

Additive manufacturing builds parts layer by layer from a digital model (STL file). No moulds or dies are needed, so tooling cost is effectively zero for a one-off part.

Fused Deposition Modelling (FDM)

Fused deposition modelling (FDM) is the most common form of 3D printing found in schools and small workshops. A spool of thermoplastic filament — typically PLA or ABS — is fed into a heated nozzle. The nozzle melts the plastic and extrudes it in precise paths across the build platform. Each layer bonds to the one below as it cools, and the platform drops slightly before the next layer is deposited. A support structure is printed under overhanging sections and removed afterwards.

FDM is ideal for concept models, ergonomic prototypes and functional parts that do not need very smooth surfaces. Typical layer thickness is 0.1–0.3 mm. The main limitations are visible layer lines on the surface and relatively low mechanical strength compared with injection-moulded parts. Consumer FDM printers such as the Bambu Lab range have made this technology genuinely accessible at under £300.

Stereolithography (SLA) cures liquid photopolymer resin with an ultraviolet laser. The build platform starts just below the surface of the resin vat; the laser traces each layer, hardening only the areas it touches. The platform then drops by one layer thickness and the next cross-section is cured. SLA produces parts with an extremely smooth surface finish and fine detail, making it popular for jewellery, dental models and appearance prototypes in product design studios. Resin is more expensive than FDM filament and uncured resin requires careful handling as a chemical irritant.

Rapid prototyping using SLA is particularly valued when a design team needs a high-fidelity model to present to a client before committing to expensive injection-mould tooling. Dyson engineers, for example, use SLA models to evaluate cyclone geometry before the tooling investment is made.

Metal Sintering

Metal sintering (also called selective laser sintering or SLS when applied to metals, or DMLS — Direct Metal Laser Sintering) spreads a thin layer of metal powder across the build platform and a laser selectively fuses the particles. Unfused powder acts as its own support structure and is recycled after the build. The result is a fully dense metal component with mechanical properties close to those of a traditionally machined part.

Metal sintering is used across aerospace, automotive and medical engineering for parts that are geometrically too complex to machine conventionally — internal cooling channels inside a turbine blade, for instance, or a lightweight titanium bracket for an aircraft seat with internal lattice structures. Rolls-Royce uses metal sintering for low-volume turbine components. The process is slow and the machines cost hundreds of thousands of pounds, so it is reserved for high-value, low-volume parts.

Key Fact

FDM (thermoplastic filament), SLA (UV-cured resin) and metal sintering (laser-fused powder) are three distinct additive routes. FDM is cheapest; SLA gives the best surface finish; metal sintering produces functional metal parts with complex geometry.

Additive Manufacturing vs Mass Production

A common error is to describe additive manufacturing as a mass-production method. It is not. The table below captures the key differences examiners reward.

Tooling cost: Additive manufacturing requires no moulds, dies or fixtures — the digital model is sent straight to the machine. Injection moulding, by contrast, requires a steel mould that can cost £20,000–£200,000 before a single part is made. Additive manufacturing therefore has zero tooling cost, making one-off and low-volume production economically viable.

Speed of iteration: A designer can update a CAD model and have a revised prototype in hand within hours. With traditional tooling, modifying a mould takes days or weeks and costs thousands of pounds. This is why product development teams use additive manufacturing for rapid prototyping during the design iteration phase.

Geometric freedom: Additive processes can produce internal cavities, lattice structures and undercuts that are impossible or prohibitively expensive to machine. Conventional subtractive machining is limited by tool access; additive is limited only by the digital model.

Production volume: Additive manufacturing is slow per part. A single FDM print of a mobile phone case takes 2–4 hours. Injection moulding cycles in 30–60 seconds. For volumes above a few thousand units, injection moulding almost always has a lower unit cost once the tooling cost is amortised.

Material waste: Additive manufacturing adds material only where needed — waste is minimal. Subtractive processes (milling, turning) can waste 90% of the starting billet for complex aerospace parts. This makes additive manufacturing more sustainable for expensive materials such as titanium.

Rapid Prototyping in the Engineering Design Process

Rapid prototyping sits between the design phase and the production phase. An engineer creates a CAD model, exports it as an STL file, and feeds it to an additive manufacturing machine. The resulting prototype is used to test fit, form and function before committing to expensive tooling. This compresses the design cycle significantly: Tesla’s Gigafactory uses additive manufacturing to iterate on manufacturing jigs and tooling fixtures at speed, avoiding the lead times of conventional fabrication. Once the design is finalised, mass production typically uses a different process — injection moulding, die casting or CNC machining — better suited to high volumes.

Thinking in Systems

Every engineered product — from a car braking system to a factory conveyor — is a system. Engineers break complicated products down into smaller, manageable pieces so they can design, build and test each part separately. The three main tools for doing this are block diagrams, schematic drawings and flowcharts. Understanding when to use each one is essential.

Key Fact

The input–process–output (IPO) model is the foundation of all system design. Every system takes something in, does something to it, and produces a result. Identifying these three stages is the first step when analysing or designing any engineering system.

The Input–Process–Output Model

The input–process–output model (IPO) lets engineers describe any system with three boxes. In an electric kettle: the input is the mains electricity and cold water; the process is the heating element converting electrical energy to heat; the output is boiling water. In a car engine: the input is fuel and air; the process is combustion; the output is rotary motion at the crankshaft.

A system also has a system boundary — an imaginary line that separates what belongs to the system from the wider environment. Drawing the boundary forces the engineer to decide exactly what is and is not part of their design.

System Block Diagrams

A system block diagram uses rectangular blocks joined by arrows to show how sub-systems connect. Each block is labelled with what it does (e.g. “temperature sensor”, “microcontroller”, “motor driver”). The arrows show the direction of signal or energy flow.

Block diagrams are NOT circuit diagrams and NOT flowcharts. A circuit diagram shows how components are wired using standard symbols (resistor, capacitor, LED). A flowchart shows the sequence of steps a process or program follows. A circuit diagram offered in place of a block diagram is unlikely to earn the marks for the block-diagram question, because it does not show the system stages the question asks for.

Key Fact

A system block diagram uses labelled rectangles and arrows only — no component symbols (resistor zigzag, capacitor plates, logic gate shapes). If the diagram looks like a circuit, it is wrong. Blocks describe WHAT each sub-system does, not HOW it is built.

Open-Loop and Closed-Loop Control

In an open-loop system the output has no effect on the process. A toaster set to a timer is open-loop: it heats for a fixed time regardless of whether the toast is burnt or pale. In a closed-loop system a sensor monitors the output and feeds information back to the controller. An oven thermostat is closed-loop: it measures actual temperature and switches the heating element on or off to match the set point.

Closed-loop systems are more accurate but more complex to design. Most industrial control systems — from a car cruise-control to a furnace temperature controller — are closed-loop because small disturbances (draughts, varying load) would cause the output to drift without feedback correction.

Large systems are broken into sub-systems. A car has sub-systems for engine management, braking, steering, lighting, infotainment and climate control. Each sub-system can be designed and tested independently. On a block diagram, sub-systems are shown as blocks that can themselves be expanded into more detailed block diagrams — this is called hierarchical decomposition.

The system boundary decides what counts as an input and what counts as an output. For a car engine management sub-system, “throttle position” is an input (from outside the sub-system, controlled by the driver), whereas “fuel injector pulse width” is an output (leaving the sub-system to control the fuel delivery).

Schematic Drawings

A schematic drawing (or schematic) uses standard symbols to show how components connect, not how they are physically arranged on a PCB or in a machine. Electrical schematics use British Standard (BS 3939) symbols: zigzag for a resistor, two parallel lines for a capacitor, a circle with an arrow for a motor. Hydraulic and pneumatic schematics use ISO 1219 symbols: rectangles for cylinders, diamonds for filters, arrows on lines for flow direction.

Schematics are the standard language of engineering workshops. If you hand a schematic to a technician, they can identify every component and trace every connection regardless of what the physical product looks like. This is why drawing interpretation is a key skill examined in the written paper.

Flowcharts show the sequence of steps in a process or control program. There are four standard symbols you must know:

  • Terminator (oval) — marks the START or END of the process. Every flowchart must begin and end with a terminator.
  • Process box (rectangle) — shows an action to be carried out, e.g. “Switch motor ON” or “Heat element for 30 s”.
  • Input/Output parallelogram — shows data entering or leaving the system, e.g. “Read sensor value” or “Display temperature”.
  • Decision diamond — asks a YES/NO question, e.g. “Is temperature > 80°C?” with two arrow paths leaving it.

Feedback loops in flowcharts must loop back to a decision diamond or an earlier process box — never to the start terminator. A common error is drawing the feedback arrow going all the way back to START, creating an infinite loop with no way to exit.

Choosing the Right Representation

The examiner expects you to choose the correct type of diagram for the question. Use a block diagram when asked to show how sub-systems relate and where signals flow. Use a schematic when asked to show component connections using standard symbols. Use a flowchart when asked to show the sequence of steps or decisions in a process or control program. Mixing these up is one of the most common reasons students lose marks on systems questions.

Analogue and Digital Signals

Electronic systems process information as signals. There are two types: analogue signals vary continuously — like the voltage from a thermistor that rises and falls as temperature changes. Digital signals have only two states: HIGH (logic 1) or LOW (logic 0). A button that is either pressed or not pressed produces a digital signal.

Most sensors produce analogue outputs. To use an analogue sensor with a digital circuit (such as a microcontroller), an analogue-to-digital converter (ADC) is needed. The ADC samples the voltage at regular intervals and converts it into a binary number. Without an ADC, the microcontroller cannot read the sensor. Examiner reports show that half of students leave ADC questions blank — memorising this definition is a guaranteed mark.

Key Fact

An ADC (analogue-to-digital converter) converts a continuous analogue voltage into a digital binary number that a microcontroller or processor can read. Sensors that produce analogue outputs (LDR, thermistor, microphone) all need an ADC to interface with digital control systems.

Sensors

Sensors are input devices that convert a physical quantity into an electrical signal. The two most common in engineering exams are:

  • LDR (light-dependent resistor) — its resistance decreases as light intensity increases. In bright light: low resistance → high current. In the dark: high resistance → low current. Used in automatic street lighting, security systems and photocopiers.
  • Thermistor — its resistance decreases as temperature increases (NTC type — negative temperature coefficient). Used in thermostats, engine management systems and fire alarms. A thermistor in a potential divider circuit produces an analogue voltage that changes with temperature.

Other sensors include pressure sensors (transducers), proximity sensors (inductive or capacitive), and sound/vibration sensors (microphones, piezo sensors). All produce an electrical signal proportional to the physical quantity they measure.

Logic Gates

Logic gates are the fundamental building blocks of digital electronic circuits. Each gate has one or more binary inputs (1 or 0) and produces a single binary output determined by a logical rule. You must be able to name the gate, draw its symbol and complete its truth table.

AND gate: output is HIGH only when ALL inputs are HIGH. Rule: “both A AND B must be 1 for output to be 1.”

NAND gate = AND + NOT. Output is LOW only when ALL inputs are HIGH; otherwise HIGH. It is the inverse of AND. NAND gates are the most common gate in integrated circuits — any logic function can be built from NAND gates alone.

NOR gate = OR + NOT. Output is HIGH only when ALL inputs are LOW; otherwise LOW. The inverse of OR. Like NAND, any logic function can be built from NOR gates alone.

XOR gate (exclusive OR): output is HIGH only when inputs are DIFFERENT (one is 0 and the other is 1). When both inputs are the same (both 0 or both 1), output is LOW. Used in comparator circuits and error-detection systems.

Passive Components: Resistors, Capacitors and Diodes

You must be able to identify these components by their circuit symbols and describe their function:

  • Fixed resistor — limits current in a circuit. Symbol: rectangular box (BS 3939 UK) or zigzag. Value in ohms (Ω). Used in series with LEDs to prevent burnout.
  • Variable resistor (rheostat) — a resistor whose value can be adjusted mechanically. Used in dimmer switches, volume controls and sensor potential dividers. Symbol: rectangular box with an arrow through it.
  • Capacitor — stores electrical charge. Polarised capacitors (electrolytic) must be connected the correct way round; non-polarised capacitors can be connected either way. Used for smoothing rectified DC and as timing components.
  • Diode — allows current to flow in one direction only. The triangle symbol points in the direction of conventional current flow; the bar is the cathode (negative terminal). Signal diodes are small and fast; rectifying diodes handle larger currents in PSU circuits.
  • LED (light-emitting diode) — a diode that emits light when current flows through it. Must be connected the correct way round (longer leg = anode = positive). Always used with a series resistor to limit current. Output devices in control panels and status indicators.
Key Fact

Common exam error: students identify a transistor symbol as a resistor. A resistor symbol is a box (or zigzag). A transistor symbol has three connections — collector, base and emitter — with an arrow on the emitter. A diode symbol is a triangle pointing to a bar. Memorise these three symbols and you eliminate a common source of lost marks.

Why Testing Matters in Engineering

Before a component leaves a factory or enters service, engineers must verify that it meets the design specification. A suspension cable on the Forth Road Bridge, a landing gear strut on a passenger aircraft, or a pressure valve on a chemical plant — all must be tested to confirm they will perform safely under load. The choice of test method depends on whether the component can be destroyed in the process or must survive to be used.

Key Fact

Destructive testing (DT) destroys the component in the process — it reveals accurate material data but the tested piece cannot be used. Non-destructive testing (NDT) leaves the component intact and usable after testing. Both are used in manufacturing quality control, but NDT is essential when every item must be tested.

Destructive Testing Methods

Tensile testing clamps a machined test piece in a tensile testing machine and applies an increasing pull until fracture. The machine records the load and extension at every point, producing a load-extension graph. From this, engineers derive yield strength, tensile (ultimate) strength, elongation at fracture and reduction in area. The test tells engineers whether a material batch meets its specification.

Hardness testing measures resistance to surface indentation. Three named methods are:

  • Vickers hardness test — a diamond pyramid indenter is pressed into the surface under a known load; the diagonal of the resulting impression is measured to calculate a Vickers Hardness Number (VHN). Suitable for all metals.
  • Rockwell hardness test — uses either a diamond cone (for hard materials) or a steel ball (for softer metals); hardness is read directly from a dial gauge as the indenter penetrates. Fast and widely used in production-line testing.
  • Brinell hardness test — a hardened steel or tungsten carbide ball is pressed into the surface; the diameter of the impression is measured to calculate the Brinell Hardness Number (BHN). Used for softer metals and castings.

Charpy impact test measures toughness — a notched test piece is supported at its ends and struck by a swinging pendulum hammer. The energy absorbed by the fracture is measured in joules. Low temperatures reduce toughness in many steels, which is why Charpy testing is critical for offshore and arctic structures.

Visual inspection is the simplest NDT method — a trained inspector examines the surface under good lighting, sometimes with a magnifying glass or borescope (an optical probe for internal surfaces). It finds surface cracks, corrosion, missing welds and damage, but only on features that can be seen.

Dye penetrant (liquid penetrant) testing detects surface-breaking cracks in clean, non-porous materials. A coloured or fluorescent dye is applied to the surface, drawn into cracks by capillary action, then a developer is sprayed on to draw the dye back out as a visible indication. Used on aluminium aircraft panels and stainless steel welds.

Ultrasonic testing (UT) sends high-frequency sound waves through a component using a transducer. Sound reflects from internal defects (voids, cracks, inclusions) and the reflected signals are displayed on a screen. UT can detect deep internal flaws invisibly and is used extensively on rail axles, pressure vessel welds and composite panels.

Radiographic testing (X-ray or gamma-ray) passes radiation through a component onto a film or digital detector. Denser material absorbs more radiation, so defects (voids, porosity, inclusions) appear as dark areas on the radiograph. X-ray inspection is standard practice for aircraft welds and medical implant castings.

Magnetic particle inspection (MPI) detects surface and near-surface cracks in ferromagnetic materials (iron, steel). The component is magnetised and fine iron particles are applied — they cluster at points where magnetic flux leaks across a crack, making the crack visible. MPI is used on gearbox housings and crankshafts.

Quality Assurance vs Quality Control

Examiners consistently note that students use these terms interchangeably — they have distinct meanings.

Quality assurance (QA) is proactive — it is the entire management system put in place to prevent defects before they occur. It includes staff training, supplier approval, maintenance schedules and documented procedures. ISO 9001 certification is a quality assurance standard.

Quality control (QC) is reactive — it catches defects that have already occurred by inspecting or testing finished or in-process components. QC activities include dimensional checks with gauges, visual inspection and destructive testing of sample components from a batch.

In practice, both are needed: QA reduces the rate of defects; QC provides the evidence that the specification has been met.

Key Fact

QA = the system to PREVENT defects (processes, training, standards). QC = the CHECKING of products to FIND defects. QA is proactive; QC is reactive. This distinction is a consistent examiner concern.

Tolerances and Gauging

No manufacturing process produces a perfectly precise dimension every time. Tolerance defines the acceptable band of variation around a nominal (target) dimension. For example, a shaft with a nominal diameter of 25.00 mm and a tolerance of ±0.1 mm may measure anywhere from 24.90 mm to 25.10 mm and still be accepted.

Tighter tolerances increase manufacturing cost because they require more precise machines, more frequent tooling changes and slower cutting speeds. Engineers balance the functional need for precision against the cost of achieving it.

Measuring instruments used in quality control:

  • Vernier caliper — measures external/internal dimensions and depths to 0.02 mm precision. The sliding Vernier scale allows fractions of a millimetre to be read off reliably.
  • Micrometer — uses a precision screw thread to measure external diameters and thicknesses to 0.01 mm. More precise than a Vernier caliper; standard in machined-component inspection.
  • Depth gauge — measures the depth of holes, recesses and slots using a probe referenced to the workpiece surface. Available as Vernier or digital versions.

A GO / NO-GO gauge is a simple, fast quality control tool that does not give a numerical measurement — it simply tells the inspector whether a dimension is within tolerance or not. The GO end is machined to the upper tolerance limit; the NO-GO end is machined to the lower tolerance limit (or vice versa for shafts vs holes).

For a shaft being checked: the GO end should slide over the shaft easily (confirming the shaft is not oversize); the NO-GO end should NOT slide over (confirming the shaft is not undersize). If the NO-GO end goes on, the shaft is rejected as too small.

GO / NO-GO gauges are used on production lines where hundreds of identical components are checked per hour — they are much faster than reading a micrometer for every component.

Why Engineering Calculations Matter

Every engineered product — from a steel bridge beam to a hydraulic press — is designed using mathematics. If the numbers are wrong, components fail. This lesson covers the essential formulas engineers use to calculate area, volume, density and pressure. Getting comfortable with these calculations — and with unit conversions — is one of the highest-scoring skills on the written exam.

Key Fact

Density: ρ = m ÷ V (kg/m³). Pressure: P = F ÷ A (N/m², also called Pascals). These two formulas appear repeatedly on engineering exam papers.

Area Formulas

Area tells you how much surface a shape occupies. Engineers need it to calculate material use, applied forces, and pressure.

  • Rectangle: A = length × width (A = l × w)
  • Triangle: A = ½ × base × height (A = ½bh)
  • Circle: A = π × radius² (A = πr²). CRITICAL: always halve the diameter to get the radius before substituting.

A common exam error is substituting the diameter directly into πr². If a circular rod has a diameter of 20 mm, the radius is 10 mm, giving A = π × 10² = 314 mm². Using 20 mm gives 1256 mm² — four times too large.

A hydraulic punch has a circular head with a diameter of 40 mm. Calculate its cross-sectional area.

Step 1 — Find the radius: r = diameter ÷ 2 = 40 ÷ 2 = 20 mm

Step 2 — Apply the formula: A = πr² = π × 20² = π × 400 = 1257 mm² (to 4 s.f.)

Answer: 1257 mm² — always include the unit.

Volume Formulas

Volume is the amount of three-dimensional space a solid object occupies. Engineers use volume to calculate the mass of components before manufacture.

  • Cuboid: V = length × width × height
  • Cylinder: V = π × r² × height (V = πr²h)

Density

Density links the mass of a material to its volume. The formula is: ρ = m ÷ V, where ρ (rho) is density in kg/m³, m is mass in kg, and V is volume in m³. You need to be able to rearrange this triangle: if you know density and volume, mass = ρ × V; if you know mass and density, volume = m ÷ ρ.

An aluminium alloy block measures 200 mm × 100 mm × 50 mm and has a mass of 2.7 kg. Calculate its density in kg/m³.

Step 1 — Convert dimensions to metres: 200 mm = 0.2 m, 100 mm = 0.1 m, 50 mm = 0.05 m

Step 2 — Calculate volume: V = 0.2 × 0.1 × 0.05 = 0.001 m³

Step 3 — Apply density formula: ρ = m ÷ V = 2.7 ÷ 0.001 = 2700 kg/m³

Answer: 2700 kg/m³ — this matches the known density of aluminium alloys, which is a good sense check.

Notice how the conversion step (mm → m) comes first, not as an afterthought. Missing the unit conversion is the single most common reason students drop the final mark on calculation questions.

Pressure

Pressure is the force applied over a given area. The formula is: P = F ÷ A, where P is pressure in N/m² (Pascals, Pa), F is force in Newtons (N), and A is area in m². A small area concentrates the same force into a much higher pressure — which is why a stiletto heel causes more damage to a wooden floor than a flat shoe carrying the same person.

A hydraulic punch exerts a force of 50 000 N through a circular head of diameter 40 mm. Calculate the pressure in N/m².

Step 1 — Find the area (in m²): r = 20 mm = 0.02 m; A = π × (0.02)² = π × 0.0004 = 0.001257 m²

Step 2 — Apply the pressure formula: P = F ÷ A = 50 000 ÷ 0.001257 = 39 776 000 N/m² ≈ 3.98 × 10⁷ Pa

Answer: Approximately 39.8 MPa. Converting to standard form (3.98 × 10⁷ Pa) is acceptable and often expected in multi-step answers.

Key Fact

Key SI prefixes: milli (m) = ×10⁻³, centi (c) = ×10⁻², kilo (k) = ×10³, mega (M) = ×10⁶, giga (G) = ×10⁹. Converting between mm and m: divide by 1000. Converting mm² to m²: divide by 1 000 000. Converting mm³ to m³: divide by 1 000 000 000.

Unit Conversions — The Non-Negotiable Last Step

Examiners consistently note that students who complete the arithmetic correctly still lose marks by leaving the answer in the wrong unit. Make unit conversion your last explicit step in every calculation. The most common conversions in engineering calculations are:

  • Length: 1 m = 1000 mm (so 1 mm = 0.001 m)
  • Area: 1 m² = 1 000 000 mm² (so 1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m²)
  • Volume: 1 m³ = 10⁹ mm³ (so 1 mm³ = 10⁻⁹ m³)
  • Mass: 1 tonne = 1000 kg; 1 kg = 1000 g

When the question says 'give your answer in N/m²' or 'in MPa', that is a signal to convert. Never skip this step.

What Is Subtractive Manufacturing?

Subtractive manufacturing starts with a block, sheet or bar of material and removes unwanted sections until the finished part remains. Every process in this lesson — sawing, shearing, laser cutting, turning, milling and drilling — is subtractive. The removed material becomes waste (swarf, chips or offcuts), so material selection and planning the cutting sequence carefully both reduce cost and waste.

Cutting: Sawing, Shearing and Laser Cutting

The simplest subtractive operations separate a workpiece into pieces. Sawing uses a toothed blade — a hacksaw in the workshop or a band saw on the factory floor — to cut through metal, timber or plastics. The teeth are set (bent alternately left and right) so the kerf (slot) is slightly wider than the blade body, preventing binding.

Shearing uses two hardened blades (like giant scissors) to cut sheet metal without a kerf. A hydraulic guillotine can shear steel plate up to 10 mm thick cleanly and quickly. Because shearing requires no cutting fluid and produces no swarf, it is economical for straight-line cuts on sheet stock.

Laser cutting directs a high-power CO₂ or fibre laser beam onto the material surface. Controlled by CNC, it can cut intricate 2D profiles in metal, acrylic and timber with very narrow kerfs (as small as 0.1 mm) and no physical tool contact. Laser cutting is ideal for prototype sheet-metal brackets and signage panels but is limited to thin sections — typically below 25 mm for mild steel.

Key Fact

Sawing produces a kerf (slot) and swarf; shearing produces a clean cut with no kerf and no swarf; laser cutting produces a very narrow kerf and is CNC-controlled, allowing complex profiles to be cut automatically.

Turning on the Lathe

A lathe rotates the workpiece while a single-point cutting tool is fed along or into the material. Key parts of the lathe that examiners test regularly are:

  • Chuck — the rotating clamp at the headstock that grips the workpiece. A three-jaw self-centring chuck grips round or hexagonal bar automatically; a four-jaw independent chuck can grip irregular shapes.
  • Tailstock — the adjustable support at the opposite end of the bed. It can hold a live centre to support long workpieces, or a drill chuck for drilling on the lathe’s axis.
  • Carriage / tool post — holds the cutting tool and moves along the bed (for parallel turning) or across (for facing).
  • Bed — the precision-machined base that ensures the carriage moves parallel to the spindle axis.

Lathe operations include parallel (cylindrical) turning (reducing diameter along the length), facing (cutting across the end to produce a flat face), taper turning (angling the tool path to create a cone), and boring (enlarging an existing hole from the inside). Cutting speed and feed rate are set to suit the workpiece material — harder metals require slower speeds and a finer feed.

Every material has a recommended cutting speed (in metres per minute, m/min) — the speed at which the cutting tool moves through the material at the point of contact. For a rotating workpiece on a lathe, this depends on both the spindle speed (revolutions per minute, rpm) and the diameter of the workpiece.

The relationship is: $$N = \frac{1000 \times v}{\pi \times d}$$ where \(N\) = spindle speed (rpm), \(v\) = cutting speed (m/min), \(d\) = workpiece diameter (mm).

Worked example: A 40 mm diameter mild steel bar is to be turned. The recommended cutting speed for mild steel is 30 m/min. Find the required spindle speed. $$N = \frac{1000 \times 30}{\pi \times 40} = \frac{30\,000}{125.66} \approx 239 \text{ rpm}$$ The lathe would be set to the nearest available speed below 239 rpm to avoid over-speed and tool damage.

Notice that a larger diameter requires a lower spindle speed to maintain the same cutting speed at the surface. If the diameter halves, the spindle speed must double. This inverse relationship is a common exam question.

Milling

Milling uses a rotating multi-tooth cutter. Unlike a lathe (where the workpiece rotates), in milling the cutter rotates and the workpiece is clamped to a table that moves in X, Y and Z directions. Milling operations include:

  • Face milling — a large-diameter cutter with many teeth sweeps across the top surface to produce a flat, smooth face. Used to true-up castings and forgings.
  • Slot milling — an end mill (a cutter with teeth on its end and sides) cuts a slot or keyway into the workpiece surface.
  • Profile milling — the CNC table follows a programmed path to cut complex 2D or 3D shapes, used heavily in aerospace for aluminium wing ribs and in automotive for cylinder-head ports.
Key Fact

On a lathe the workpiece rotates and the tool is stationary (moves linearly). On a milling machine the cutter rotates and the workpiece is clamped to a moving table. Getting this the wrong way round is a common exam mistake.

Drilling

A pillar drill (also called a drill press) holds a drill bit in a rotating chuck and feeds it vertically into the workpiece. Tool names examiners expect you to know:

  • Centre drill — a short, rigid combined drill-and-countersink used first to create a precise starting point, preventing the twist drill from wandering.
  • Twist drill — the standard helical drill for producing through-holes and blind holes. Flutes carry swarf out of the hole.
  • Countersink — a conical cutter that bevels the top of a hole so a countersunk screw sits flush with the surface.
  • Counterbore — a stepped cutter that enlarges the top of a hole to receive a cap-head bolt so its head sits below the surface.

The sequence for drilling a precision hole is: mark out the centre with a centre punch → use a centre drill to start the hole accurately → drill the through-hole with a twist drill at the correct speed → de-burr the hole edges. Giving “drill” alone in an answer is not specific enough; always state the type of drill bit.

Chemical etching is used to produce printed circuit boards (PCBs). The process is subtractive but uses chemistry rather than mechanical cutting. A blank PCB consists of a fibreglass substrate coated in a thin copper layer. The desired circuit pattern is printed onto the copper using UV-sensitive etch-resist film, which is exposed and developed. The board is then immersed in ferric chloride (iron(III) chloride) solution, which dissolves the unprotected copper while leaving the resist-covered tracks intact. After etching, the resist is removed, revealing the finished copper tracks. Chemical etching bridges the Manufacturing and Systems units because PCBs are the foundation of electronic circuits.
